title: Why Are Teenagers Always Tired?
passage: Do you find it hard to get up in the morning? It's not because you're lazy. Scientists say that teenagers' bodies want to fall asleep later and wake up later than adults' bodies. Most teenagers need eight to ten hours of sleep, but many get only six or seven. Phones make the problem worse, because the light from the screen tells your brain it's still daytime. So what can you do? Try to go to bed at the same time every night, and leave your phone outside your bedroom.

title: The Girl Who Built a Beach Robot
passage: When Lena Petrova was thirteen, she went on holiday to the seaside and was shocked by how much plastic there was on the beach. 'I couldn't stop thinking about it,' she says. Back home, she started reading about the problem online, and after a few months she had an idea: a small robot that could collect rubbish from beaches. Her first robot was made from an old toy car and a kitchen sieve. 'It looked terrible, and it broke after ten minutes,' she laughs. But Lena didn't give up. Two years and twelve robots later, her design won a national science competition for young people. Now a company wants to build her robots for real. Lena, who is now fifteen, hasn't decided what she wants to do after school. 'Maybe engineering,' she says. 'Or maybe something completely different. I'm still only fifteen!'

topic_en: Blog: the new kid at school
title: Surviving My First Week
passage: Moving to a new school in the middle of the year is nobody's dream. When my family moved to Kazan last January, I was terrified. I didn't know anyone, and on my first day I walked into the wrong classroom — twice. By lunchtime I was ready to go home and never come back. Then something unexpected happened. A girl called Dasha sat next to me in the canteen and asked if I liked anime. I did! We talked for the whole break and found out we were both obsessed with the same series. The next day she introduced me to her friends, and by Friday I had a group to sit with. So here's my advice if you're the new kid: don't wait for people to come to you. Find one small thing you have in common with someone. It's much easier than you think.

title: Signal Lost — a review
passage: I started watching Signal Lost because everyone at school was talking about it, and I wasn't disappointed. The series follows four teenagers in a small town where, one morning, every phone and computer suddenly stops working. At first it seems like a fun adventure — no online homework, no messages from parents! But soon the friends realise that something much stranger is going on. The best thing about the series is the characters. They feel like real teenagers: they argue, they make silly jokes, and they make mistakes. The special effects are impressive too, especially in the last episode. My only complaint is that the middle of the season is a bit slow — episodes four and five could easily be one episode. Still, I watched all eight episodes in one weekend, and I can't wait for season two.

title: Did Your Phone Just Buzz?
passage: Have you ever felt your phone vibrate in your pocket, checked it, and found no new messages? If so, you're not alone. Scientists call this 'phantom vibration syndrome', and some studies suggest that up to 90% of phone users have experienced it. Why does it happen? Our brains are constantly trying to predict what is going on around us. If you're waiting for an important message, your brain becomes extra sensitive, so it may 'translate' a small movement of your clothes into a vibration. In other words, your brain would rather make a mistake than miss something important. Is it dangerous? Not really — experts say it's a normal reaction, not an illness. However, if it happens very often, it might be a sign that you're thinking about your phone too much. One simple solution is to switch notifications off for a few hours a day. Your brain will thank you.
